props.title: The Smiling Lieutenant

sections.content: Ernst Lubitsch's pre-Code masterpiece The Smiling Lieutenant exemplifies the sophisticated sexual comedy that defined the "Lubitsch Touch." Maurice Chevalier stars as a flirtatious Vienna military officer whose wayward wink at his girlfriend accidentally charms a visiting princess, leading to a series of delightfully risqué complications. The film showcases Lubitsch's signature style that would influence romantic comedies for decades, alongside contemporaries like Trouble in Paradise (1932) and Design for Living (1933). The innuendo-laden dialogue and subtle visual suggestions pushed boundaries while maintaining an air of elegant wit. sections.content: The musical elements in The Smiling Lieutenant demonstrate the early sound era's experimentation with the form, particularly in its use of songs to advance the plot rather than merely as entertainment interludes. Chevalier's performance style, developed in French music halls, bridges European and American sensibilities - a hallmark of Lubitsch's Hollywood work. The film's treatment of sexuality feels remarkably modern, especially compared to the more rigid Production Code era that would begin just three years later with films like It Happened One Night (1934). SUBHEAD: The Pre-Code Musical Comedy

The Smiling Lieutenant sits at a fascinating crossroads of film history, as Hollywood transitioned from silents to talkies. Its sophisticated approach to adult themes aligns it with other daring pre-Code works like Baby Face (1933) and Red-Headed Woman (1932). The film's treatment of marriage, fidelity, and female sexuality - particularly in Claudette Colbert's character's transformation - demonstrates the freedom filmmakers enjoyed before strict censorship. The famous "Jazz Up Your Lingerie" number perfectly encapsulates this era's playful approach to suggestive material.
